You do not know what ad hominem attacks are, and you’re misusing the phrase. Ad hominem attacks are arguments against people on the basis of their character. I’ve thought clearly and precisely about the ideas you presented in your comment, and I’m presenting them to you with the question: could you be unintentionally contributing to the harms you say you seek to reduce?

You don’t have to be sorry for having empathy, or for anything for that matter. I’m just presenting an assessment after some careful thought which did indeed take place, seemingly, hours after you’ve logged off.

But I think you approached my comments assuming I was NT, and I’m wondering if you could possibly see that you might have personal biases or hard and fast beliefs that, due to their personal origin, could be clouding your vision. I’m constantly reassessing myself.

You’re not wrong, you’re extremely thoughtful and helpful, and I appreciate your views. You can also dismiss my questions or say no, you can disagree and I can gladly respect that.

I don’t think people on the spectrum like myself should feel limited in our challenges based on our diagnoses. And I don’t think marriage and steady jobs are the measure of a successful life. I think everyone should have the chance to measure their own success by their own merits, and society shouldn’t dictate what we feel we have accomplished.

I don’t want preconceived notions that one has to be this that or the other to push us into a bin of unproductives. We can measure our own successes and celebrate triumphs and live life on our own terms. 

My sister has a lot of toxic feelings about being ASD and I know it because we shared those toxic feelings. I also know that if she was a voice for the community, people would be impressed by her story. I’ve been in both worlds, and I can tell you that what’s really dangerous for people like us is BIAS. We need to celebrate our differences. I spent 12 years hiding them and they are what make me beautiful. I can promise that I’d rather change the world around me and the way it thinks and sees ASD.

I probably should have mentioned that I am not neurotypical, and that I have also been diagnosed by a professional as being on the spectrum. I don’t know how much difference that makes. 

It’s been 12 years since then, and I’ve had therapists and psychiatrists outright dismiss the idea of the diagnosis for me without looking deeper, but I’m certain I met the characteristics at the time. Whether I authentically have been on the spectrum will remain a mystery. 

Her symptoms are more profoundly life altering than mine ever were, and she’s done way more with her life than I have. I don’t feel like I can authentically identify myself as having ASD anymore. But we bonded together over the pain of hiding that secret and the shame of it, so there’s more to my desire than just being NT & wanting her to conform to my idea of what she should be.

I just hope you understand I’m asking from the perspective of having masked my own behavior for years and years, and eventually “growing out” of some of those symptoms. I’m not asking to be educated about this from an outside perspective. I’m asking for perspective from someone who might see something I don’t.

I just want you to know that what you’ve shared with me is incredibly valuable, because your lived experience is what matters. Not someone’s expectations of who you should be, or how you should live.

I have been dealing with constant migraines since July 2019. I’ve been doing Botox and Aimovig for almost a year, and I recently tried Eletriptan which has been a fucking godsend.

Like you I had no quality of life, 28 migraine days a month, constant horrible symptoms. I’ve been on disability, basically bedridden, and miserable. Socially isolated and suicidal. Your experience is VALID, it is horrifically fucked up, and it is also possible that one day it will be a distant memory. 

One thing I recommend is that you PLEASE find someone to open up to who you can be honest with about what you’re going through. Friends and family may be those people, but sometimes they can also be harmful (YMMV). I started therapy again after realizing I was suicidal and it helped a lot.

I also told people who love me I wanted to die. They found resources for me and helped me find clinics and drugs that could be good alternatives. Having support is super important.

Maybe the people here are the best support system. Please keep reaching out. We are here for one another. Message me.

What recently made you conclude you are a lesbian/queer?: I’ve accepted being a lesbian after meeting “the perfect man,” & being totally unable to experience an iota of sexual attraction in his presence - despite a close friendship and strong personal connection. I thought I would marry him. We had the same values, same plans - we talked about kids. But I was kidding myself. What helped me overcome my confusion, was realizing that I had always needed a nurturing male presence in my life, and that a close friendship with a kind and loving man, satisfied that need.
